page_title: Let's code a TCP/IP stack, 4: TCP Data Flow & Socket API

sources.entry: Part 4: TCP Data Flow & Socket API

summary.title: Let's code a TCP/IP stack, 4: TCP Data Flow & Socket API
summary.one_liner: You learn how TCP tracks sent and acknowledged data with sequence-number variables, how connections close with FIN and RST, and how the BSD Socket API exposes TCP to applications.
takeaways: TCP keeps a Transmission Control Block per connection, tracking SND.NXT, RCV.NXT and SND.UNA to manage sequence numbers and ACKs.
Data transfer advances sequence variables by the segment's payload length, and the receiver acknowledges it.
Closing a connection normally takes four segments (FIN, ACK, FIN, ACK), and RST aborts it abruptly.
The BSD Socket API (socket, connect, write/sendto, read/recvfrom) hides TCP internals such as retransmission and reassembly from applications.
Tracing curl with strace shows the socket calls behind a simple HTTP GET, which can be reproduced in a minimal client.
summary.summary: This part of a series building a TCP/IP stack explains the Transmission Control Block and the sequence and acknowledgment variables that drive TCP data transfer. It walks through a tcpdump example of a data segment being acknowledged, then covers connection termination with FIN, half-close, and RST. The post then introduces the BSD Socket API as the application interface, traces the system calls of curl with strace, and builds a minimal HTTP GET client on top of the stack. The next installment is said to cover window management and retransmission timeouts.
